chunks: DC gain of an op-amp. The question: What is the DC gain of an ompamp?
The DC gain of an op-amp is how much it amplifies very slow signals. Open loop, it is huge: from about 100,000 to a million.
But in a real circuit, what matters is the closed-loop gain, which feedback sets with resistors. The op-amp's own gain just has to be big enough to make the error small.
Think of a powerful but sloppy motor steering a car while you watch the road and correct.
You keep correcting until the car is where you want it, so your eyes, not the motor, set the path. A stronger motor just leaves a smaller leftover wobble.
The feedback resistors are your eyes, and the op-amp's open-loop gain is the motor.
Two op-amps with the same 1 megahertz GBW but different DC gain.
The higher- A 0 part has its pole at 1 hertz instead of 10 hertz, so at any frequency above 10 hertz their gains are identical.
Extra DC gain buys accuracy only at very low frequency. The phase falls to minus 90° by about ten times the pole frequency.
Open-loop DC gain ( A 0 ): the gain with no feedback at zero frequency. Closed-loop gain: the gain set by the feedback network.
Loop gain: the open-loop gain divided by the closed-loop gain. It sets the error. Dominant pole: the low frequency where the gain starts to fall.
dB: 20 times the log of the gain ratio. 100,000 is 100 decibels.
Take A 0 equals 100 000 and a closed-loop gain of 10. The loop gain is 100 000 over 10 equals 10 000 , so the gain error is about 1/10,000, or 0. 01%.
For a closed-loop gain of 1000 the loop gain is only 100, so the error is about 1%.
Also, a 1 megahertz GBW with this A 0 means the gain starts falling at 1 megahertz over 100 000 equals 10 hertz. That is the whole idea.
"Open loop, an op-amp's DC gain is very large, typically 10 to the 5 to 10 to the 6 , or 100 to 120 decibels, though it's loosely specified.
In a circuit what matters is the closed-loop gain, set by the feedback resistors: 1 over beta , such as 1 plus R f over R g .
The finite open-loop gain only adds a small error of about G over A 0 , so a gain of 10 on a 10 to the 5 part is off by 0. 01%.
And that high gain only holds at low frequency: a dominant pole rolls it off at 20 decibels per decade down to unity at the GBW."
